title: The Colditz Cock — the glider POWs built in a Nazi castle attic
sources: Wikipedia: Colditz Cock — a glider built by British prisoners of war at Oflag IV-C, Colditz Castle, Germany; Lieutenant Tony Rolt noticed the chapel roof line was hidden from the guards and could launch a glider across the River Mulde, about 60 m below; Bill Goldfinch and Jack Best led the work with 12 assistants (the 'apostles'), using the two-volume 'Aircraft Design' by C. H. Latimer-Needham found in the prison library; they built it in the lower attic above the chapel behind a false wall, with lookouts and an electric alarm; over thirty ribs, mostly from bed slats; wing spars from floorboards; control wires from electrical wiring in unused parts of the castle; skinned with blue-and-white checked prison sleeping bags sealed with boiled German ration millet; wingspan about 10 m (32 ft); weight 110 kg (240 lb); it was to be launched from a 20 m runway of tables by a falling bathtub full of concrete; the take-off was planned for spring 1945, but the Americans liberated the prisoners on 16 April 1945 before it flew; war correspondent Lee Carson took the only photograph of it in the attic; its fate is unknown; a full-size replica flew successfully at RAF Odiham in 2000 with Goldfinch and Best watching, and in March 2012 a radio-controlled replica launched unmanned from the same roof crossed the river and landed safely in a meadow.

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / Imperial War Museum): Colditz Castle; the glider in the attic (Lee Carson, 15 April 1945); prisoners at Oflag IV-C; the plan of Oflag IV-C; a playing card hiding an escape map; the replica
Archive film (public domain): Polygoon newsreels of early glider flights in the Netherlands (1931, 1936); US Army 'The Big Picture: Airborne to Battle' (WWII gliders) — illustrative
Music: It's a Long Way to Tipperary, public domain

post.facebook:
In a Nazi castle prison, British officers secretly built a full-size glider in the attic — out of bed slats and sleeping bags.

Colditz Castle was the Germans' special prison for officers who had already escaped from somewhere else, perched on a cliff above a river. But one prisoner noticed the guards couldn't see the chapel roof — and from there you could fly over the river 60 metres below. With a book on aircraft design from the prison library, behind a fake wall in the attic, with lookouts and an electric alarm, they built it: ribs from bed slats, wing spars from floorboards, control wires stolen from the castle's own wiring, and a skin of blue-and-white prison sleeping bags sealed with boiled millet. Ten metres wide, two seats — launched by a bathtub full of concrete dropped through the floor.

By spring 1945 it was almost ready, kept as a last resort in case the SS tried to massacre the prisoners. Then the Americans arrived. It never flew; one photo was taken, and it vanished. But in 2000 a replica flew with its builders watching — and in 2012 a remote-controlled copy launched from the same roof crossed the river and landed safely.

Would you have climbed in? 👇

youtube.description:
In a Nazi castle prison, British officers secretly built a full-size glider in the attic — out of bed slats and sleeping bags.

The Colditz Cock: at Oflag IV-C, Colditz Castle, Tony Rolt spotted that the chapel roof was hidden from the guards. Bill Goldfinch, Jack Best and their 'apostles' built a two-seat glider behind a false wall — ribs from bed slats, spars from floorboards, control wires from the castle's wiring, skinned with prison sleeping bags sealed with millet — to be launched by a falling bathtub of concrete. The Americans liberated Colditz on 16 April 1945 before it flew. A replica flew in 2000, and in 2012 a radio-controlled copy launched from the same roof crossed the river and landed safely.
